l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L08: Database concepts.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Define table, record, field and key field and identify them in a given table. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

A database is an organised collection of related data, stored so that it can be searched, sorted and presented quickly. Almost every organisation in Northern Ireland uses one: schools keep pupil details and attendance, GP surgeries keep patient records, shops keep stock levels and sports clubs keep member lists. Inside the database, data is held in tables. A table stores data about one type of thing, for example members, and is laid out in rows and columns.
Makes sense. Keep going.

A database package also gives tools to work with the data. Queries find the records you need, forms make it easy to enter and edit data, reports present the results neatly, and macros automate jobs that are done again and again. Tables can be linked by relationships so that each fact only needs to be stored once. In this lesson you will learn the key terms that the exam expects you to define and to spot in a table.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Each row in a table is a record: all of the data about one person or item, such as one swimmer in a club. Each column is a field: a single item of data that is stored for every record, such as Surname or DateOfBirth. The column heading is the field name, and each field is given a data type. The key field, also called the primary key, is the field that uniquely identifies each record.
Got it. Keep going.

No two records can have the same key value and it cannot be left blank. Codes such as MemberID or PupilID make good key fields because the organisation creates them to be unique. Names, dates of birth, phone numbers and towns make poor key fields because two people can share them. Sometimes no single field is unique, so two fields are used together; this is called a composite key, for example MemberID and SessionDate in a table of lesson attendance.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

A flat file keeps all the data in one table. This often means the same details are typed many times, which is called data redundancy. It wastes space and causes errors, because one copy may be updated while another is not. A relational database avoids this by splitting the data into several tables, each about one thing, and linking them. The link is made by storing the primary key of one table in the other table, where it is called a foreign key.
Okay. Keep going.

For example, MemberID is the primary key of Members and a foreign key in Lessons. This is a one-to-many relationship: one member can book many lessons. Other types are one-to-one and many-to-many. Enforcing referential integrity on the relationship keeps the tables consistent. It stops a lesson being booked for a member who does not exist, and stops a member being deleted while bookings still point to them, unless cascade delete is switched on.
Go on.

Tables store the data, but users rarely work with tables directly. A query is a question asked of the database. It checks every record and returns only those that meet the criteria, for example all Junior squad members born after 2011. A query can use fields from more than one linked table and can sort the results. A form is an on-screen layout used to enter new records, edit existing ones or view records, usually one at a time.
Right. Keep going.

Forms are easier to use than a table, can include drop-down lists, buttons and the club logo, and can combine fields from more than one table while saving each item to the correct table. They also help keep data accurate by limiting what can be typed. A report presents data from a table or query in a formatted layout ready for printing or display. Reports can group similar records, sort them and calculate totals or counts, for example a register of members grouped by squad.
Go on.

A macro is a small stored program that performs a set of database actions automatically. Instead of carrying out several steps every time, the user clicks one button on a form and the macro does the work. Macros can open a form, run a query, print a report, or add, update or delete a record. These four record jobs are sometimes called CRUD: create, read, update and delete. Macros save time, reduce mistakes and let staff with little database knowledge use the system safely.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Importing data means bringing data into the database from another file rather than typing it again. A common example is importing a csv file or a spreadsheet worksheet, such as a list of new members exported from an online sign-up form. Importing is quicker and avoids typing errors. Before importing, the data should be checked so that column headings match the field names, values suit each field's data type and there are no duplicate key values.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Database?
An organised, structured collection of related data that can be searched, sorted and presented, usually held in one or more tables.
Table?
A database structure that stores data about one type of thing, organised in rows (records) and columns (fields).
Flat file?
A database that holds all its data in a single two-dimensional table, which often leads to repeated data.
Record?
All of the related data about one object or person, forming a complete row in a table. A record is made up of fields.
Field?
A single item of data stored about every object or person, forming a column in a table and identified by its field name.
Key field or primary key?
A field whose value is unique for every record, used to identify each record in a table.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Database questions appear on nearly every Unit 1 paper, often worth 8 to 11 marks: the 2019 paper, question 3, the 2021 paper, question 2, the 2022 paper, question 10, the 2023 paper, question 3, the 2024 paper, question 3 and the 2025 paper, question 5. You are often given a table and asked to name a record, a field or the key field, or to fill in missing field names. When asked to choose a key field, name it and justify it: the value is unique for each record. Say why other fields are unsuitable, for example two customers could have the same surname. For relationship questions name the type, usually one-to-many, and say which table is the 'one' end. Questions on database tools and key term matching test whether you can tell a query, form, report and macro apart, so learn a clear one-sentence definition of each. A common mistake is saying a report searches for data; it is the query that searches and the report that presents the results.
Let's finish with a question for the listeners. A swimming club stores Surname, Squad, DateOfBirth and MemberID. Which is the best key field? Is it A, MemberID; B, Surname; C, Squad; D, DateOfBirth?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is A: MemberID. MemberID is created to be unique for every member. Names, squads and dates can be shared.
